body.text: Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will hold the balance of power in the state for the next four years.
While Labor and the Liberals have spent recent days travelling across the state in big campaign buses to critical seats, the parties will pause their travels today out of respect for Remembrance Day.

How potholes are shaping the election campaign

Nowhere has the impact of potholes on the Victorian election been clearer than in Forest Hill in Melbourne's east, where a pothole at the intersection of Canterbury Road and Mahoneys Road became a political battleground.

Local residents complained about potholes at the intersection, some of which had grown to a depth of 15cm. An Instagram page was even set up for the pothole earlier this month, providing daily updates.
Whitehouse City Council pleaded with the state government to fix potholes at the intersection following complaints from residents.

Forest Hill falls into the electorate of Glen Waverley, which unexpectedly flipped to Labor in 2022. Holding the seat by a margin of just 3.3 per cent, the electorate is shaping up to be a major battleground in the election.
The Liberal Party seized on the opportunity, with Opposition Leader Jess Wilson holding a press conference at the pothole to attack Labor's record on roads.
The tactic spurred the Carroll government into action, with the potholes being repaired in the days after Wilson's visit.
Whitehorse City Council celebrated the win and thanked the state government for the much-needed repairs. The pothole's Instagram account had to say farewell for the time being.
Key Event
One Nation does not support free abortion pledge
Victorian One Nation leader Warren Pickering says the party does not support free abortion pledges from the major parties, describing the plans as "stupid".

During an interview on broadcaster Neil Mitchell’s podcast, Pickering was asked if One Nation would block legislation related to free abortion care in the upper house if the party holds the balance of power after November.
"You’re damn right I would," Pickering said. "It’s stupid. Taxpayers should not be paying for abortions."
"You’re damn right I would," Pickering said.
"It’s stupid. Taxpayers should not be paying for abortions."
It’s important to note that providing free abortion care would not require a change in Victorian legislation.
Seats in focus: Box Hill

Labor narrowly won Box Hill throughout the 1980s but after a redistribution it became a relatively strong seat for the Liberals. For 26 years, between 1992 and 2018, the seat was held by prominent Liberal moderate Robert Clark, who was the attorney-general and finance minister in the Baillieu and Napthine governments.

Despite Clark’s long tenure he was sensationally defeated at the 2018 election by Labor’s Paul Hamer. In 2022, Hamer secured a swing towards him and in April 2026 he was elevated to cabinet in Jacinta Allan’s final reshuffle before she was deposed three months later.

The seat is home to the second-largest proportion of Chinese-born residents in the state. Its steady population growth has been driven by overseas migration, and the suburb of Box Hill has had the most new apartment builds approved out of any eastern suburb of Melbourne. Box Hill, as well as Burwood on the southern border of the seat, will also be home to two of the six stations on the eastern section of the Suburban Rail Loop.

Box Hill lies at the upper range of the 16 seats the Coalition would be looking to win to form majority government. Labor has heavily invested in this fast-growing area and the Liberal Party has struggled for support in the Chinese community in recent years. This will likely be an important seat for both parties to win.
Policy in focus: Potholes
The state of Victoria's roads and the growing number of potholes has become a key issue in the coming election.

As the ABC's Kate Ashton reported in September, the proportion of state-managed roads in poor or very poor condition increased from 39 to 48 per cent between 2021 and 2024, according to an auditor-general report.

And the human toll of Victoria's crumbling roads was brought into focus after the death of a 71-year-old motorcyclist who crashed after reportedly hitting a pothole on the Western Highway near Ballarat.
The public backlash to potholes led to Premier Ben Carroll admitting in August that the condition of Victoria's roads was "not good enough".
Each political party is pledging to improve Victoria's roads if elected this month.

Labor pledged to double the number of potholes fixed this year from 250,000 to 500,000 with a fresh $352 million investment, while also piloting a program to have minimum-security prisoners perform roadside maintenance.
The Coalition has promised to boost current spending on road maintenance by 25 per cent, pledging $5 billion to repair 1 million potholes across Victoria.
The Greens say if elected, the party will bring VicRoads back into government hands, diverting money saved with public ownership into fixing the state's roads.

And One Nation has promised to publish the condition and funding of every major regional road and create a public pothole portal for Victorians to make reports, with locked-in maintenance funding for regional roads.
Greens set sights on seat in Melbourne's north
In many parts of the seat of Northcote, about 7km north of Melbourne's CBD, political messaging sits alongside bustling cafes and gentrification.
Aside from its brief dalliance with Senator Lidia Thorpe, the seat has been Labor for almost a century and swung back that way in 2018.
In 2022, Labor won the seat by just 184 votes. This year, the contest is shaping up to be just as close.
Pause in campaigning for Remembrance Day
With the nation pausing for reflection today on Remembrance Day, the major parties' media campaigns are also taking a breath.
Premier Ben Carroll and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson are not doing any major media events today, but that doesn't mean MPs and candidates aren't out campaigning locally.

Homelessness an important election issue according to survey
New research by RMIT suggests a large number of Victorians rate homelessness as a very or extremely important election issue.
The RMIT survey, commissioned by St Vincent de Paul Society Victoria, shows 89 per cent of those surveyed supported increased government funding of homelessness prevention programs.
Around 65 per cent of respondents believe cost of living is a leading cause of homelessness and 50 per cent say it's their most important voting issue.
The survey polled 650 Victorian residents on their views about homelessness-specific issues.
RMIT noted that the respondents were younger, more educated and more metropolitan than the general population.
Vinnies is using the research to call for parties to commit to a three-year homelessness prevention package ahead of the election.

"Keeping people housed is cost-of-living relief, and we need a long-term plan for it," says Ray Kelleher from Vinnies. "Homelessness is a vote-shifter for nearly two in three (64 per cent) Victorians telling us they would be more likely to vote for a party with a commitment to increasing investment into homelessness, and prevention programs are the leading priority for funding."

The Coalition announced yesterday it will preference One Nation above Labor, the Greens and Socialists on its how-to-vote cards in some electorates.
Meanwhile, Labor will run an open ticket in inner-city Melbourne seats, where it faces strong competition from the Greens.
It's created outrage among some of our audience members, while others (namely Preference Pete) are less concerned.
Greens accuse Labor of 'dodgy' preference deal
Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell has accused Labor of doing a "dodgy backroom deal" by depriving the minor party of preferences in the hard-fought seat of Prahran.

As the ABC revealed yesterday, Labor will run an open ticket in the inner-city seat, which includes the suburbs South Yarra and Windsor. This means Labor will not direct supporters where to put their remaining votes on the ballot.
Prahran always goes down to preferences, so Labor's how-to-vote cards here have significant flow-on effects for Opposition Leader Jess Wilson's chances of forming majority government.

Labor has previously given its preferences to the Greens here, which helped the minor party claim the seat. But the Greens lost Prahran last year when Labor sat out a by-election, denying them the necessary preferences.
Greens candidate Angelica di Camillo is attempting to unseat local Liberal member Rachel Westaway.
Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said Labor's decision to run an open ticket was "frankly unforgivable".
"After months of scaremongering about a Liberal-One Nation government, Labor is now using its preferences to help elect one," Sandell said.

"This could be one of the most consequential elections in the state's history. The result may come down to a single seat, and a divisive party like One Nation could hold the balance of power. It is frankly unforgivable that Labor would do a dodgy backroom deal to help elect a Liberal-One Nation government — and it's something that Victorian voters will not easily forget."
Seats in focus: Berwick

Berwick was recreated ahead of the 2022 election from parts of Bass, Narre Warren South and the now-abolished seat of Gembrook. Its original incarnation existed between 1976 and 2002 and was always held by the Liberal Party.

Brad Battin became the member for Gembrook in 2010, defeating a two-term Labor MP with a 7.35 per cent swing towards him. The redistribution of 2021 saw more than one-third of Battin’s Gembrook constituents transferred to the reconstituted Berwick, including the seat's most Liberal-friendly areas. Battin followed along and was re-elected to parliament.

After the election, he contested the leadership of the party against John Pesutto, losing by a single vote. When Pesutto lost the high-profile defamation case brought against him by upper house Liberal member Moira Deeming, Battin successfully moved a spill motion and won the leadership against Chris Crewther and Jess Wilson.

Battin's time as leader started strong, with the Liberals gaining the seat of Prahran in a by-election then achieving their highest levels of polling support in the entire term. But his relentless focus on crime and lukewarm relations with factional heavyweights created tensions that came to a head in October 2025, when a shadow cabinet reshuffle saw key backers in the previous year's leadership spill demoted. Battin was booted from the leadership a month later and replaced by first-term MP Jess Wilson, who he had promoted to shadow treasurer in the reshuffle.
Greens pledge health funding for Richmond
The Greens have promised $1.75 million to expand the Community Paramedics program in Richmond if elected.
The program is currently piloted by North Richmond Community Health and funds free pop-up clinics run by qualified paramedics near Richmond's public housing towers.
The Greens' proposed funding would expand the program to other sites across Richmond.
Richmond MP Gabrielle de Vietri says the proposal is a "common-sense solution" to providing health care.
"Everyone deserves good health care, no matter their income or where they live. We're proud to back an innovating local program and help bring it to more people across Richmond," de Vietri says.
The Greens won the seat of Richmond in 2022 following decades of Labor dominance, and hold it with a 7.3 per cent margin.

Polling place closures hit 36 Victorian towns

Residents in central Victoria say the closure of three local polling booths is a "kick in the teeth" for rural communities, with voters facing longer trips to cast their ballots in the upcoming state election.
An analysis of Victorian Electoral Commission data has revealed 36 regional towns that had a polling booth at the 2022 state election will no longer have one within 5 kilometres.
In nine of those towns, the nearest voting centre is at least 10km away for this election.

Seats in focus: Bentleigh
Bentleigh has a long history as a bellwether held by the governing party for nearly all of the last 60 years. This means Labor has won it at five of the last six elections this century.

Current MP Nick Staikos has achieved the highest shares of the two-candidate preferred vote in Bentleigh since the seat’s first occupant, Bob Suggett, a Liberal. He has also risen higher in the government than any other member for the seat, serving in the ministry since 2024. He is currently the housing minister and was formerly the minister for the Suburban Rail Loop.
After a tight win in 2014, Staikos secured one of the highest swings in the state towards him in Labor’s 2018 landslide and his vote largely held up in 2022.

But the seats on the Frankston train line, which have had a big role in determining government, have more Liberal-leaning demographic traits the closer they are to the city centre. Bentleigh is the closest of the four and has the 17th-highest personal incomes in the state compared to 56th-ranked Frankston at the end of the line.

Staikos’s ministerial responsibilities overlap with issues that will likely be important in this district: the government’s housing policy in growth corridors like Bentleigh and the Suburban Rail Loop, which sits just outside its boundaries.

Greens lash Labor over Prahran preferences
The Victorian Greens have released a scathing rebuke of Labor's decision to deny the party preferences in the key election seat of Prahran.
Labor had previously given its preferences to the Greens, which helped the party claim the inner south-east Melbourne seat in 2014.
Liberal MP Rachel Westaway now holds the seat, after winning it by a slim margin in a 2024 by-election.
Yesterday, Labor confirmed it would run an open ticket, meaning it would not direct its supporters where to put their remaining votes on the ballot.
Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell says the preference arrangement is shocking considering the election could be one of the most consequential in the state's history.
"This is Labor admitting that they have more in common with One Nation and the Liberals than they do with the Greens — because the Greens want real change," she said.
